```{r, include = FALSE}
has_gtsummary <- requireNamespace("gtsummary", quietly = TRUE) &&
  utils::packageVersion("gtsummary") >= "2.1.0"
has_cardx <- requireNamespace("cardx", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A select-all-that-apply question is one question answered once per
respondent, but survey exports store it as one 0/1 column per option. Treating
those columns as independent variables, or pivoting them to long rows, gives
wrong numbers. checkboxr keeps the data wide, sets the whole question to `NA`
when a respondent gave no usable answer, and summarizes each option as a row
under one question header.

The pipeline is: **define, check, clean, summarize**.

```{r setup}
library(checkboxr)
```

## The data

`cb_example` has eight respondents and one checkbox question, "Transport
used". Each row exercises one rule.

```{r}
cb_example
```

Respondent 4 ticked "don't know", 5 ticked "prefer not to answer", 6 ticked
nothing, and 7 ticked both "car" and "don't know".

## Two ways to get it wrong

**Zeros that are not real zeros.** Three people use a car. Dividing by all
eight respondents gives 37.5%, but respondents 4, 5 and 6 told us nothing
about their transport. Their zeros are missing answers, not "no".

```{r}
mean(cb_example$q5_car)
```

**Long data.** Pivoting to one row per tick duplicates respondents. The table
N becomes the number of ticks, and every other variable is distorted:
respondents with two ticks count twice and respondents with none disappear.

```{r}
ticks <- cb_example[c("id", "age", "q5_car", "q5_bus", "q5_bike", "q5_none", "q5_dk", "q5_pna")]
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ticks)[-(1:2)], function(col) {
  ticks[ticks[[col]] == 1, c("id", "age")]
}))
nrow(long)            # 10 rows for 8 respondents
mean(long$age)        # 41.4
mean(cb_example$age)  # 42.4, the true mean
```

## Define

A *set* says which columns belong to the question, how to label them, and
which columns mean "none of the above", "don't know" and "prefer not to
answer". Every remaining column is a substantive option.

```{r}
sets <- cb_sets(
  cb_define(
    name = "q5", label = "Transport used",
    cols = starts_with("q5_"),
    option_labels = c(q5_car = "Car", q5_bus = "Bus", q5_bike = "Bike",
                      q5_none = "None of the above"),
    none = q5_none, dk = q5_dk, pna = q5_pna
  )
)
sets
```

`cols` is tidyselect and is resolved against the data each time the sets are
used.

The columns do not have to be 0/1. `TRUE`/`FALSE`, `"Yes"`/`"No"`,
`"Checked"`/`"Unchecked"` and similar codings are recognised on their own.
For anything else, such as 1 = yes and 2 = no, say so with `checked` and
`unchecked`. If your export leaves unticked boxes blank, add
`blank = "unticked"`. See `?cb_define` for the full list.

With many questions, `cb_detect()` drafts the sets from the column names. It is
a starting point to review, not something to use blindly.

```{r}
draft <- cb_detect(cb_example, sep = "_")
```

## Check

`cb_check()` counts how many respondents fall under each rule, without
changing anything.

```{r}
cb_check(cb_example, sets)
```

One "don't know", one "prefer not to answer", one respondent with nothing
ticked and one conflict. It also stops with an error if a column holds
anything other than ticked, unticked or `NA`.

## Clean

`cb_clean()` gives each respondent one status per set and sets the
substantive and "none" columns to `NA` for everyone whose status is not
`answered`.

```{r}
cleaned <- cb_clean(cb_example, sets)
cleaned
```

The rules, first match wins:

| Pattern in the raw row | Status | Substantive and none columns |
|---|---|---|
| Any set column is `NA` | `not_shown` | `NA` |
| Substantive option ticked with dk, pna or none | see `conflict` | see `conflict` |
| dk ticked, no substantive option | `dk` | `NA` |
| pna ticked, no substantive option | `pna` | `NA` |
| none ticked, no substantive option | `answered` | kept |
| At least one substantive option ticked | `answered` | kept |
| Every box unticked | `skipped` (`empty = "na"`) or `answered` (`empty = "zero"`) | `NA` or kept |

Two decisions are yours:

* `empty`: is an all-unticked row a skip (`"na"`, the default) or a real
  "none of these" (`"zero"`)? A set with a "none of the above" option makes
  the default safe.
* `conflict`: when "don't know" is ticked next to a real option, `"keep"`
  (default) trusts the real option, `"na"` discards the row, and `"error"`
  stops so you can look at the rows.

```{r}
mean(cleaned$q5_car, na.rm = TRUE)                                   # 3 of 5
mean(cb_clean(cb_example, sets, conflict = "na", quiet = TRUE)$q5_car, na.rm = TRUE) # 2 of 4
mean(cb_clean(cb_example, sets, empty = "zero", quiet = TRUE)$q5_car, na.rm = TRUE)  # 3 of 6
```

The `q5_dk` and `q5_pna` columns are never changed, and cleaning twice gives
the same result as cleaning once.

```{r}
identical(cb_clean(cleaned, sets, quiet = TRUE), cleaned)
```

## Summarize

`cb_tbl_summary()` passes the wide, cleaned data to
`gtsummary::tbl_summary()` and groups each set under one header. Sets are
named in `include` next to ordinary columns.

```{r, eval = has_gtsummary}
library(gtsummary)

cb_tbl_summary(
  cleaned, sets,
  include = c(age, q5),
  type = age ~ "continuous",
  statistic = age ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
  label = age ~ "Age"
)
```

The table N is 8, the number of respondents. The option percentages use the
five respondents who answered the question, which is the `n` in the header.
Anything in `...` goes to `tbl_summary()`.

`show_status = TRUE` adds the status below the set, with the full sample as
the denominator, so non-response is reported and not hidden.

```{r, eval = has_gtsummary}
cb_tbl_summary(cleaned, sets, include = q5, show_status = TRUE)
```

The result is an ordinary gtsummary table. With `by`, the answered count
differs by column, so it is dropped from the header.

```{r, eval = has_gtsummary && has_cardx}
cb_tbl_summary(cleaned, sets, include = c(age, q5), by = group,
               type = age ~ "continuous") |>
  add_overall() |>
  add_p()
```

`add_p()` tests each option on its own, as if the options were unrelated
variables. That ignores the dependence between options of one question. For
a joint test of a multiple-response question, see the MRCV package.

## Helpers

```{r}
cb_count(cleaned, sets)     # substantive options ticked
cb_collapse(cleaned, sets)  # ticked labels as text
```

`cb_long()` gives one row per tick. It exists for plotting only. Never pass
its output to `tbl_summary()`: that is the long-data mistake from the top of
this page.

```{r}
cb_long(cleaned, sets)
```
